articles.excerpt: Most indie Chrome extensions burn money on backend proxies and headless browsers from day one. When I built ShopScope (a Chrome Manifest V3 extension that inspects any Shopify storefront's theme, inst…
articles.body: Most indie Chrome extensions burn money on backend proxies and headless browsers from day one. When I built ShopScope (a Chrome Manifest V3 extension that inspects any Shopify storefront's theme, installed apps/pixels, and SKU pricing), I flipped that constraint: zero backend compute, zero AI token bills, and strict minimal permissions. Because every inspection runs inside the user's active browser tab, it unlocks a clean Freemium -> $39 Lifetime Pro model without worrying about heavy power users eating server margin. 1.

articles.title: How Do You Get Different AI Tools to Work Together?
articles.excerpt: Here's a setup I suspect a lot of you have right now. Claude Code is open in one terminal. Codex is open in another because it handles a certain kind of refactor better. The spec was hammered out in a…
articles.body: Here's a setup I suspect a lot of you have right now. Claude Code is open in one terminal. Codex is open in another because it handles a certain kind of refactor better. The spec was hammered out in a ChatGPT thread last Tuesday. The decision about which endpoint to deprecate is buried in Slack. And the result of all of it eventually shows up as a GitHub PR that you have to review by hand. Every one of those tools is good. None of them knows the others exist. So you become the integration layer. You copy the context out of one window and paste it into another. You re-explain the spec to the second agent. You relay the decision from Slack. You remember which agent already tried what. You are the router, the shared memory and the reviewer, all at once.

articles.title: AI Image to Video Under the Hood: Choosing Reference Frames, Motion Budgets, and Models for Short Clips
articles.excerpt: Animating a still image with an AI image to video model looks deceptively simple from the outside: upload a PNG, type a sentence, and get a five-second MP4 back. In practice, creators and indie builde…
articles.body: Animating a still image with an AI image to video model looks deceptively simple from the outside: upload a PNG, type a sentence, and get a five-second MP4 back. In practice, creators and indie builders who try to use these clips in real projects hit the same failure modes over and over: faces drift halfway through a turn, hands blur during gestures, text warps, and camera pans invent bizarre background geometry. Most of those artifacts have predictable causes. Treating image-to-video generation like a constrained engineering pipeline - starting with the right reference frame, setting a realistic motion budget, and matching the shot to the right video model - turns hit-or-miss renders into repeatable clips. 1.

articles.title: Backtesting Indian stocks against random portfolios: how I built Tickjury
articles.excerpt: Tickjury is a website where I backtest trading ideas on Indian stocks and put up the results. I also put up the failed results. In this post I’m going to talk about the architecture of the site and ab…
articles.body: Tickjury is a website where I backtest trading ideas on Indian stocks and put up the results. I also put up the failed results. In this post I’m going to talk about the architecture of the site and about one specific design decision I made, which is the use of a random portfolio as a baseline for comparisons. The problem with a backtest Whenever you do a backtest and see a good yearly return, the question to ask is, what would have happened had I randomly picked a portfolio in the same years? In Tickjury, for every trading model, I compare with the NIFTY 500 and also with 20 randomly selected portfolios from the same list of stocks. The portfolio is selected to match the model in terms of timing, stake size and costs, but the stock pick is random.

articles.title: 'Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home' at 40: 'Trek' has never been as joyous or fun as in 'the one with the whales'
articles.excerpt: Colorful metaphors, a near-miss with Eddie Murphy and humpback whales in 20th-century California.
articles.body: It may have been subtitled "The Voyage Home", but to most viewers "Star Trek IV" (which has just turned 40) will always be "the one with the whales". After "The Wrath of Khan" and "The Search for Spock" went to some pretty dark places — ear worms, the destruction of the Enterprise, the death (and later resurrection) of a certain beloved Vulcan — the franchise was in need of some light relief. So what better than to set coordinates for the then-present day of 1986 San Francisco, for a time-travel comedy romp? Spock himself, Leonard Nimoy, had directed "The Search for Spock" and Paramount had lined him up to call the shots on a follow-up before the movie had even landed in theaters.
